594 Epilogue
theorem If a is a real number, then one and only one of the following conditions holds:
(i) ot = 0,
(ii) a is in P,
(iii) —a is in P.
PROOF If a contains any positive rational number, then a certainly contains all negative
rational numbers, so a contains 0 and a =/ 0, i.e., a is in P. If a contains no
positive rational numbers, then one of two possibilities must hold:
(1) a contains all negative rational numbers; then ot = 0.
(2) there is some negative rational number x which is not in a; it can be assumed that x is not the least element of Q — a (since x could be replaced
by x/2 > x); then —ot contains the positive rational number —x, so, as we
have just proved, —ot is in P.
This shows that at least one of (i)—(iii) must hold. If ot = 0, it is clearly impossible
for condition (ii) or (iii) to hold. Moreover, it is impossible that a > 0 and —a > 0 
both hold, since this would imply that 0 = a + (—a) > 0. |
Recall that ot > fi was defined to mean that ot contains /f, but is unequal to fi.
This definition was fine for proving completeness, but now we have to show that
it is equivalent to the definition which would be made in terms of P. Thus, we
must show that a — fi > 0 is equivalent to a > fi. This is clearly a consequence
of the next theorem.
THEOREM If a, fi, and y are real numbers and a > fi, then a + y > fi + yPROOF The hypothesis a > fi implies that fi is contained in a; it follows immediately from
the definition of + that fi +y is contained in a +y. This shows that ot +y > fi+y.
We can easily rule out the possibility of equality, for if
ot + y = fi + y,
then
ot = (a + y) + (_y) = (fi + y) + (_y) = fi,
which is false. Thus ot + y>fi + y.]
Multiplication presents difficulties of its own. If ot, fi > 0, then ot • fi can be
defined as follows.
Definition. If ot and fi are real numbers and a, fi >0, then
ot • fi = {z : z < 0 or z. = x • y for some x in ot and y in fi with x, y > 0}.
THEOREM If ot and fi are real numbers with a. fi > 0, then a • fi is a real number.
